title: Why your backtest is lying to you: How including delisted coins saved my strategy from a false sense of security
author: Beautiful_Tart_1802
selftext:
Hey everyone,  
I wanted to share a hard lesson I learned while developing my own local desktop backtester in Python—and how fixing it completely changed my results.  
Most of us build strategies, run them on the current top 100 or 500 coins on TradingView or other platforms, see a gorgeous upward equity curve, and think we’ve found the holy grail. But there’s a massive silent killer in algorithmic trading: **Survivorship Bias**.  
**The Trap of Survivorship Bias:**  
When you backtest only on coins that are actively trading today, you are testing a survivor-biased dataset. You completely ignore hundreds of tokens that pumped hard, rugged, or slowly bled to zero and got delisted. If your strategy traded those dead coins during your historical window, your backtest missed every single one of those catastrophic liquidations. Your historical win rate and profit factor look artificially inflated because you're only looking at the "winners" that survived.  
**How I solved it for myself:**  
To get an honest stress test, I built a local Python app that explicitly filters out coins listed after my test period, and—crucially—pulls **delisted USDT perpetual contracts** using exact historical candles and official delisting dates.  
**The Real-World Results:**  
When I ran a batch test across 500+ coins (including the dead/delisted ones) over a multi-year period on my modest 8GB RAM ultrabook, it took about 5–6 hours. And the reality check was brutal:  
 The equity curve looked much more realistic (and rougher) than the "sugar-coated" tests.  
 It exposed hidden flaws in my risk management—specifically how the strategy handled sudden liquidity drying up before a delisting.  
 Cross-checking the indicator logic against TradingView showed identical execution, but now with true, unskewed market data.  
 I exported the detailed trade logs into an AI assistant, which broke down my performance across every single dead coin in minutes.  
(Bonus: The app also handles live execution via APIs for major global exchanges like Bybit, Binance, and OKX).  
If you’re backtesting strictly on current top lists, your strategy might be walking into a minefield. Has anyone else found a clean way to handle historical delistings in your pipelines? Would love to hear your approaches!

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Great point, and including the dead coins is the part most people skip. Along the same line, I'd build the coin list as it was on each test date instead of today's list, and drop anything too thin to trade at that time. Exits near a delisting are also worth modeling with wider slippage, since you often can't get out at the last candle's price. Cymetica's Backtest Labs includes fees and can hold out the last part of the history, which helps with the fresh-data check on top of that.

comments.author: Born_Jaguar_5946
comments.body: Ignoring delisted coins is basically letting the market choose your historical winners for you. No wonder the equity curve looks incredible. The same data selection problem can distort directional strategies evaluated for moon. A backtest that excludes failed assets isn't measuring the strategy you could realistically have traded.
